steps.tx: **Graves disease** causes diffuse thyrotoxicosis with a high radioiodine uptake, TSH-receptor antibodies, and sometimes orbitopathy or pretibial myxoedema. A toxic nodule or toxic multinodular goitre has focal or patchy uptake and no TSH-receptor antibodies. The drawing shows receptor autoantibodies on the TSH receptor, a diffuse goitre, Graves ophthalmopathy, tremor, tachycardia, and pretibial myxoedema.

steps.tx: **Painless thyroiditis**, iodine exposure, and exogenous thyroid hormone are all causes of low uptake. Factitious thyrotoxicosis has a low thyroglobulin, whereas thyroiditis has a high thyroglobulin. Antithyroid drugs do not treat thyroiditis. The scan row is drawn as a dark diffuse Graves pattern, a patchy multinodular pattern, and a faint thyroiditis pattern.

steps.tx: **Methimazole** is the **preferred** antithyroid drug except in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm, when propylthiouracil is preferred. Propylthiouracil also blocks peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, but it can cause severe liver injury, so it is not long-term first-line therapy. Both drugs can cause a rash and both can cause agranulocytosis, so the warning is the same whichever thionamide you choose.

steps.tx: **Agranulocytosis** from an antithyroid drug presents with fever and sore throat. Stop the drug and do not restart either thionamide, because the reaction can cross. Routine blood counts do not replace that warning. Tell every patient to stop the tablet and seek a count the same day if the throat is sore and a fever is present. A mild rash is a different problem and is not agranulocytosis.

left.title: Agranulocytosis
points: Stop the drug the same day
Do not switch to the other thionamide

steps.tx: **Radioiodine** is **contraindicated** in pregnancy and during breastfeeding. It can worsen thyroid eye disease, so active moderate or severe orbitopathy is a reason to choose surgery or an antithyroid drug instead. If radioiodine must be used in milder active eye disease, glucocorticoid cover is given. A pregnancy test is confirmed before the dose in any person who could be pregnant.

nodes.label: Mild active disease: steroid cover if radioiodine

steps.tx: A **beta blocker**, often propranolol, is started for symptomatic thyrotoxicosis because it relieves adrenergic symptoms and propranolol also slows T4 to T3 conversion. It does not treat the underlying gland. The drawing marks tachycardia and tremor, which are the symptoms a beta blocker is for. Continue the antithyroid drug, because the heart rate will return when the tablet is stopped if the gland is still overactive.

right.title: Thionamide
points: Does not empty stored hormone at once

steps.tx: **Thyroid storm** is a clinical diagnosis. A Burch-Wartofsky score of 45 or higher is highly suggestive. Treat with a thionamide first, propylthiouracil if it is available, then iodine, a beta blocker, and glucocorticoid, and treat the precipitant. Never give iodine before the thionamide, because iodine given first can fuel more hormone synthesis. Supportive care includes cooling and treatment of the infection or the surgery that set it off.

steps.tx: **Subclinical hyperthyroidism** is treated when the TSH is below 0.1 mIU/L in patients older than about 65 years, or when heart disease or osteoporosis is present. Beta blockade alone is not enough when the TSH stays fully suppressed and the risk is high. A TSH between 0.1 and the lower reference limit is a milder band, and treatment is individual. Repeat the TSH before you ablate a gland for one slightly low result.
